Issued at 502 AM CDT Sun Sep 27 2026

Benign southwest flow aloft over the Northern Plains this 
morning, with an occluded cyclone over central Canada and an 
upper trough digging into the Pacific coast. A cold front 
attendant to the Canadian occluded cyclone has nearly stalled 
from the northern Red River Valley to near Lake Oahe. Light 
winds and high RH just ahead of the front had allowed patchy 
dense fog to develop from around Lake Oahe to the southern 
James River Valley, but the fog has been consistently clearing 
from north to south since the middle of the night. Radar imagery
also shows scattered showers over southwest North Dakota, with 
a few thunderstorms in northwest South Dakota. Little to no rain
appears to be reaching the ground on the North Dakota side of 
the border though, as observed cloud bases have mostly remained 
above 10 kft.

Surface high pressure building off the Northern Rockies should 
eventually push the cold front further east today. A secondary 
cold front is forecast to sag into northern parts of the state 
today, but will likely stall before reaching I-94. This gives a 
high temperature forecast today of around 60 degrees northwest 
to 70 degrees southeast. The forcing mechanism responsible for 
the high- based showers in southwest North Dakota early this 
morning appears to be a plume of ~700 mb theta-e advection. 
This moisture transport is forecast to slowly translate 
eastward through the day, which could maintain the scattered 
showers. Any rainfall amounts through the afternoon are 
expected to be minimal.

The Pacific coast trough will begin inducing low level warm air
advection and moisture transport over the Northern High Plains 
later tonight, while also ejecting a shortwave from the Great 
Basin to the Northern Plains. Chances for showers steadily 
increase this evening through tonight, and by early Monday 
morning, widespread showers with scattered embedded 
thunderstorms are expected across much of western and central 
North Dakota. This initial round of showers and storms may begin
to clear the forecast area from west to east by midday, but 
there is uncertainty in how quickly a second round of showers 
and storms could develop, and how widespread it could be, over 
central North Dakota Monday afternoon as the left exit region 
of an upper level jet streak approaches from the southwest. The
upper level divergence could spread over a quasi-stationary 
frontal boundary that is attendant to both the origins of the 
cold front moving through eastern parts of the region this 
morning and lee cyclogenesis near the Black Hills, but there is 
latitudinal uncertainty on where this frontal boundary could 
settle. From Monday evening through Monday night, lingering 
showers and storms should be confined to the warm/moist sector 
of the lee cyclone from south central into eastern North Dakota 
where the low level jet could also assist with maintaining 
convection.

There is a wide array of potential outcomes in the intensity 
and coverage of thunderstorms late tonight through Monday night.
For the initial round late tonight through Monday morning, 
thunderstorms should remain elevated above a shallow but stable 
boundary layer with access to around 500-1000 J/kg MUCAPE and 
modest mid level lapse rates around 7 C/km. Deep layer shear 
will be strong, but that is driven by easterly to southerly 
flow in the lowest 1 km AGL underneath a prevailing southwest 
flow in the mid to upper levels. It is therefore likely that 
any updrafts will experience a lower amount of effective bulk 
shear, but it could still approach 30 kts. UH tracks in both the
HREF and REFS are short and barely touch the 75 m^2/s^2 mark 
that tends to be an indicator of severe convection. This leads 
to a most likely outcome of scattered strong thunderstorms of a 
pulse nature across southwest and central North Dakota through 
Monday morning, with hail being the main hazard (aside from 
heavy rain and lightning). 

The Monday afternoon through Monday night time period carries 
much greater uncertainty. First, there is the question of where 
the quasi- stationary front will end up during the afternoon, 
which deterministic models indicate could be as far south as 
between I-94 and the SD border or as far north as along Highway 
2. This may determine the most likely corridor for afternoon 
convection. Another question is whether there will be a capping 
inversion above a moist but conditionally unstable boundary 
layer. The degree of CIN could vary over both space and time 
and may ultimately be driven by breaks in cloud cover. Forecast
CAPE has generally remained in the 500-1000 J/kg range, but 
there is meridional uncertainty in where a plume of locally 
higher buoyancy could set up in southern North Dakota. There is
